name: Buyang, Langjia variety
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Sagart, Laurent. 2004. The higher phylogeny of Austronesian and the position of Tai-Kadai. Oceanic Linguistics 43(2): 411-444; HAL author manuscript halshs-00090906, reporting Langjia Buyang data 'from Li Jinfang 1999' (李锦芳 1999 布央语研究, 北京: 中央民族大学出版社). Corroborated by Edmondson, Jerold A. [c. 2002-2004 draft] 'Kra or Kadai languages' (pre-print of the chapter in Diller, Edmondson & Luo (eds.) 2008 The Tai-Kadai Languages, Routledge), also 'taken from Li 1999'.
catalog_locator: Sagart 2004 HAL manuscript printed folios 30-31 (paragraph beginning 'To remove any lingering misconceptions' starts on p. 31, whose printed folio is 30, and ends on p. 32, folio 31); Table 6 on p. 51 (printed folio 50); Edmondson draft p. 9, 'Word structure' paragraph.
catalog_quote: To remove any lingering misconceptions that the resemblances between Tai-Kadai and Austronesian are due to chance, I give below comparisons involving Buyang, a recently-described Tai-Kadai language from the Kra branch, spoken near the China-Vietnam border (data from Li Jinfang 1999). While TK languages generally reflect An disyllables as monosyllables (either by losing the first syllable, or by collapsing the two), Buyang is remarkable in that it preserves several An disyllables as disyllables (Table 6). Observe that in these words, the first syllable is reduced: the vowel is always /a/, the syllable is toneless ('tone zero'), and the inventory of initial consonants is limited to a few: m- (for An m- and w-), q- (for An q- and k-), t- (for An C- and t-). Yet Buyang shows that An words in Proto-TK were still disyllabic. ... [Table 6: Disyllabic An words in Buyang] die ma0 tɛ54 ... eye ma0 ta54 ... bird ma0 nuk11 ... 8 ma0 ðu312 ... head qa0 ðu11 ... louse qa0 tu54 ... fart qa0 tut54 ... raw qa0 ʔdip54 ... bear (n.) ta0 mɛ312 ... cover (v.) ta0 qup11 [Sagart 2004]. ... Word structure. The discussion of the grammatical features of Buyang is taken from Li 1999. Buyang words often reflect a sequi-syllabic structure with the first syllable being toneless. [Edmondson draft, p. 9]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No opened source uses the word 'stress' for Langjia/Langnian Buyang. What is stated (Li 1999 via Sagart 2004 and Edmondson draft; Li 1999/2002/1998 snippets and abstracts in Chinese) is that the language is tonal (Langjia: six tones 33, 24, 31, 312, 54, 11) and that the prefix/presyllable of sesquisyllabic words is reduced, vowel a, and carries no tone (轻声 'neutral/light tone', tone 0; 33 in slow speech), so the full tone and prominence sit on the final major syllable. That is a tonelessness statement, not a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Li & Luo 2010 (Paha, not Langjia): some prefixes vary between a phonemic tone and the neutral tone; Li 1998 abstract: prefixes read 33 in slow speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic lexical words: prefix + major syllable); statements are second-hand from Li 1999 (Langjia). The only first-hand text held by the project (Li & Luo 2010) is Paha Buyang, a different ISO language [yha].
new_statements.identity_note: Langnian Buyang [yln] = the Langjia 郎架 (郎念土语: Langjia + Nianlang villages, Gula township, Funing) variety of Eastern Buyang, the variety Li Jinfang 1999 布央语研究 describes in detail (Li 2003 abstract; Glottolog alt. names Langjia, Langjia Buyang). All open first-hand Buyang descriptions held by the project (Li & Luo 2010 PL 607, Li & Luo 2006 LTBA, Li 1996) are of Paha/Baha Buyang [yha] = baha1256, and Ostapirat 2000 uses Ecun = E'ma Buyang [yzg] = emab1235; the Sagart 2004 and Edmondson statements quoted here are explicitly from Li 1999 (Langjia) and carry Langjia tone values.

tone_statements.citation: Li Jingfang [Li Jinfang 李锦芳] & Zhou Guoyan 周国炎. 1998. Diachronic evolution of initial consonants in Buyang. Mon-Khmer Studies 28: 115-135.
tone_statements.quote: b, d, g in Baha have become unaspirated voiceless stops p, t, k in other dialects. In Langjia, words with initial stops p, t, k have the feature of voiced glottal fricative in low tones. It is thus clear that the time when initial voiced stops became devoiced was not too long ago. [footnote:] Here we use tone categories for the Kam-Tai languages, e.g. 'chaff': Kam (Dong) pa6, Sui pja6, etc., but the phonetic value of tones for such languages as Gelao, Pubiao, Laki Buyang

sources.note: Abstract: '布央语前缀由一个音节构成，大多为CVT型.. 韵母多为a，声调多念轻声，慢读为中平33' (prefix syllables mostly carry the neutral/light tone, mid-level 33 in slow speech). Not a stress statement.
